worker_b_evidence.section_or_page: 2.2 Electrochemical Performances and First-Principles Calculations of Hydrogel Electrolytes
worker_b_evidence.verbatim_quote:
At the 1:1 ratio, the balanced interplay among strong SA–Zn2+ coordination, weak PVA–Zn2+ coordination, and abundant hydrogen bonds effectively disrupts the solvation sheath of Zn2+, lowering the desolvation energy barrier. Excessive SA leads to overly tight binding, while excessive PVA introduces chain entanglements that hinder ion transport. This lower desolvation energy not only promotes uniform Zn deposition by mitigating concentration polarization but also minimizes parasitic Zn2+ consumption during cycling.

To elucidate the interfacial interactions within the SA/PVA electrolyte and the atomic-scale distribution of Zn2+, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed. As shown in Figure 3e, the electrostatic potential (ESP) distribution across the carboxyl groups of the SA hydrogel, the hydroxyl groups of the PVA hydrogel, and the hydration region is inhomogeneous. This non-uniform ESP may establish an electrostatic gradient along the polymer chains, facilitating the directional migration of hydrated Zn2+ ions along the charged functional groups. The binding energy between the SA/PVA composite and Zn2+ (−47.29 kJ mol−1) is significantly more negative than those of SA–Zn2+ (−22.25 kJ mol−1), PVA–Zn2+ (−17.82 kJ mol−1), and H2O–Zn2+ (−7.01 kJ mol−1), indicating a stronger affinity of the composite hydrogel for Zn2+. This enhanced binding promotes structural stability by modulating coordination inter- actions (Figure 3f). Furthermore, the energy levels of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) were calculated to assess the electron- donating capabilities among all components (Figure 3g). The SA/PVA system exhibits a narrower energy gap and a higher relative HOMO energy, suggesting superior electron transfer capability and facilitating easier electron donation to absorbed Zn2+ ions.

1. Introduction

Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) have garnered significant attention as potential future

energy storage solutions due to their cost-effectiveness and environmental friendliness,

primarily leveraging water as an electrolyte [1]. However, a significant challenge hindering

their practical advancement lies in the limitations associated with the use of zinc (Zn) metal

electrodes as anodes [2,3]. In particular, the surface chemistry and physical conditions of the Zn

---

## Page 3 (MAIN)

metal anode encounter several challenges when interfacing with water for energy storage

purposes. The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and metal corrosion can result in unstable

surface chemistry during AZIB operation [4,5]. Furthermore, during the deposition and

stripping process, the uneven deposition of Zn ions on the surface of the Zn metal anode implies

selective and partial electrochemically active sites on the anode [6,7]. This often leads to the

formation of physically sharp and protruding Zn dendrites, which can damage cells, trigger

short circuits, and result in low electrochemical cyclability [8,9]. These anode problems

critically affect the surface properties of Zn metal anodes and hinder the full potential and

feasibility of AZIBs. To address these problems, the application of innovative coatings and

protective layers on the Zn metal anodes has emerged as an effective method to promote

favorable surface chemistry and physical conditions [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. To focus on the

challenges associated with the surface properties of the Zn metal anode in AZIBs, several

parameters must be considered during the development of coating materials [13]. These

parameters include ion conductivity, electrochemical inertness along with Zn ions, mechanical

strength (fracture toughness), and processability [[14], [15], [16], [17]]. Coating materials should

be ionically conductive to facilitate charge carrier transfer and exhibit high electrochemical

inertness to prevent side reactions and consumption while maintaining a high concentration of

available Zn ions. In terms of mechanical stability, the requirement for coating materials with

high fracture toughness is greatly emphasized because of the significant stress variations

experienced by Zn dendrites during charge-discharge cycles [18]. Moreover, this coating

configuration must offer high mechanical strength to withstand severe protrusion from Zn

dendritic growth. Finally, for convenient and practical applications, uniform deposition and

ease of processability of coating materials are crucial. This is because the bare surface of the Zn

metal anode between coating materials can inadvertently serve as unfavorable surface sites

where chemical side reactions and physical issues occur harshly.

Various strategic coating materials have been employed for the surface modification of Zn metal

anodes, including the application of conductive polymers or inorganic materials. Polymer

coatings such as polyamide (PA) [19], polyacrylamide (PAM) [20], polypyrrole (PPy) [21], and

polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) [22] effectively regulate the ion stability of Zn ions and mechanical

strength but they encounter challenges in achieving high ionic conductivity. Moreover,

organic-related artificial layers can also be regarded as promising coating candidates to

enhance the electrochemical performance and corrosion resistance of Zn metal anodes [23,24].

However, these organic artificial layers also face certain challenges, especially related to

mechanical strength. While conductive polymers such as PPy offer advantages in enhancing

ionic conductivity [25,26], they often exhibit insufficient mechanical strength to effectively

address physical issues. This limitation stems from the need for high crystallinity in polymer

materials to achieve high mechanical strength, which restricts polymer chain ion mobility and

---

## Page 4 (MAIN)

high ion conductivity. Furthermore, efficient deposition methods and precise layer deposition

with high uniformity on Zn metal anodes are relatively less effective than other coating

material candidates. In contrast to polymers, conductive inorganic materials offer several

advantages, including high ionic conductivity, applicability, and mechanical rigidity [27,28].

However, they tend to fracture during charge-discharge cycles and struggle to accommodate

volume changes [29], resulting in a loss of conformal contact and continuous protection of the

Zn metal anode. Furthermore, these materials can easily form alloys with Zn ions through

irreversible side reactions, leading to high consumption of Zn ions during electrochemical

cycles. Consequently, to synergistically harness the benefits of both organic and inorganic

coating materials, hybrid organic-inorganic heterostructure coating materials can effectively

accommodate the challenges of Zn anodes in AZIBs, which exhibit high ionic conductivity,

chemical inertness, applicability, and flexibility [[30], [31], [32]]. Moreover, the necessity of

elasticity in the coating layers used in batteries is crucial for their ability to adapt to the volume

changes during charge and discharge processes [33,34]. Conductive polymers like PPy generally

lack adequate mechanical strength to address physical challenges, whereas AgNWs exhibit

excellent elastic stiffening properties [35,36]. The combination of AgNWs and PPy results in a

composite material with the necessary mechanical flexibility. Therefore, the Ag/PPy

nanocomposite more effectively inhibits dendrite formation due to the superior mechanical

strength of the AgNW core compared to PPy.

In this study, we propose a novel organic-inorganic hybrid coating composite that

synergistically enhances the surface chemistry and physical endurance of Zn metal anodes.

These composites feature silver nanowires (Ag NWs) as the core, surrounded by polypyrrole

(PPy), which is a π-conjugated polymer (Ag/PPy). The Ag NWs, synthesized via a polyol

method, serve as a conductive core material, offering high applicability, ionic conductivity, and

rapid diffusion paths owing to their nanostructured design. Moreover, the surface of the Ag

NWs is encapsulated by PPy, which acts as a protective shell layer. This shell layer not only

improves the electrochemical inertness of the Ag NWs but also provides mechanical flexibility

to address the physical challenges. After modification with Ag/PPy Zn protection layers

(Ag/PPy-ZPL) on the Zn anode, the electrochemical performance of the Ag/PPy-ZPL Zn|| Ag/PPy-

ZPL Zn symmetry cell has been largely improved for 10C rate charge-discharge conditions.

Moreover, the rate capability and long-cycle stability of the Ag/PPy-ZPL Zn||α-MnO battery

have been significantly enhanced. The Ag/PPy-ZPL Zn achieves a high discharge-specific

capacity of up to 302 mAh/g at a current density of 0.5 A/g. Moreover, the battery maintains a

high capacity retention rate of approximately 95 % after 300 cycles at a discharge current of 0.5

A/g with a high coulombic efficiency (CE) approximately 99.49 %.

worker_b_evidence.verbatim_quote: The organic cations with hydrophobic alkyl chain groups can enable electrostatic adsorption on the Zn surface, which can not only create a hydrophobic interphase on Zn to suppress the water- induced side reactions but also homogenize the electric field distribution to guide uniform Zn2 + deposition. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements at various scan rates are conducted to measure the EDL capacitance of Zn//Zn cells with different electrolytes (Figures 1f and S4 ) [ 30 ]. Compared to the baseline and inorganic cation containing electrolytes, the hydrophobic organic cation-based electrolytes demonstrate much higher EDL capacitance (e.g., 36.0 µF cm− 2 for ZS, 51.3 µF cm− 2 for ZS-NH4 + , and 141.5 µF cm− 2 for ZS-Pmim+ ), due to the electrode-philic adsorption of organic cations on the Zn surface. The activation energies ( Ea ) of different electrolytes are determined by the Arrhenius plots of temperature-dependent charge transfer resistance ( Rct ) measured in symmetrical Zn//Zn cells (Figures 1g and S5 ). Ea can be obtained from the slope by linearly fitting ln(1/ Rct ) versus 1000/T [ 38 ]. The Ea of ZS-Pmim+ (28.8 kJ mol− 1 ) is the lowest among all electrolytes, which is markedly lower than those of ZS-TEA+ (31.2 kJ mol− 1 ), ZS-NH4 + (34.8 kJ mol− 1 ), ZS-Na+ (35.3 kJ mol− 1 ), and pristine ZS (38.2 kJ mol− 1 ) (Figure 1h ).
